questions.q: The magnitude and direction of the acceleration produced in a body of mass $5$ kg when two mutually perpendicular forces $8$ N and $6$ N act on it, are respectively :
questions.solution:
Given forces are $F_1 = 8$ N and $F_2 = 6$ N acting perpendicular to each other.

The magnitude of the net force is $F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2} = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$ N.

The magnitude of acceleration is $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$ m s$^{-2}$.

Let $\theta$ be the angle made by the net force with the $8$ N force.

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{F_2}{F_1} = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$ with the $8$ N force.

Answer: $2$ m s$^{-2}$; $\tan^{-1}(3/4)$ with $8$ N force

questions.q:
A box of mass $15$ kg is kept on the floor of a stationary trolley. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the trolley is $0.12$. Keeping the box in stationary state over the trolley, the maximum acceleration with which the trolley can be moved horizontally in m s$^{-2}$ is :
($g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the trolley be $a$.

In the frame of the trolley, a pseudo force $ma$ acts on the box in the direction opposite to the motion.

For the box to remain stationary relative to the trolley, the static friction force must balance this pseudo force.

The maximum static friction force available is given by $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$.

Equating the pseudo force to the maximum static friction force gives the maximum acceleration:

$ma_{\text{max}} = \mu_s mg$

$a_{\text{max}} = \mu_s g$

Substituting the given values $\mu_s = 0.12$ and $g = 10$ m/s$^2$:

$a_{\text{max}} = 0.12 \times 10 = 1.2$ m/s$^2$

Answer: $1.2$

questions.solution:
For minimum wear and tear on the tyres, the frictional force should be zero. The required centripetal force is provided entirely by the horizontal component of the normal reaction.

The optimum speed $v$ on a banked road is given by:

$v = \sqrt{R g \tan \theta}$

Squaring both sides:

$v^2 = R g \tan \theta$

Substituting the given values $v = 10$ ms$^{-1}$, $R = 50$ m, and $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$:

$(10)^2 = 50 \times 10 \times \tan \theta$

$100 = 500 \tan \theta$

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{100}{500} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)$

Answer: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)$

questions.q: A particle of mass \(m\) is at rest at the origin at time \(t=0\) It is subjected to a force, \(F(t)=F_0 e^{-b t}\) in the \(x\)-direction. Its speed \(v(t)\) is depicted by which of the following curves?
questions.solution:
Given \(\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{FO} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\), acceleration \(\mathrm{a}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{t}) / \mathrm{m}=(\mathrm{FO} / \mathrm{m}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\),
so \(dv/dt=(\mathrm{FO} / \mathrm{m}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\).
Integrating with \(\mathrm{v}(0)=0\) gives \(\mathrm{v}(\mathrm{t})=(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb}))\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\right]\).
This rises from 0 and asymptotically approaches \(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb})\).
Hence the correct \(\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{t}\) curve is a rising exponential saturating at \(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb})\), which corresponds to (b).

The Reason is false because friction's work isn't always negative - the sign depends on the direction of displacement relative to the friction force (static friction can even do positive work in some cases).

Assertion : A block of weight 10 N is pushed against a vertical wall by a force of 15 N. The coefficient of friction between the wall and the block is 0.6. Then, the magnitude of maximum frictional force is 9 N.
Reason : For given system block will remain stationary.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
- Normal reaction from the wall equals the horizontal push: \(\mathrm{N = 1 5 ~ N}\), so maximum static friction f_max \(=\mu \mathrm{N}=0.6 \times 15=9 \mathrm{~N}\) (Assertion true).
- To remain at rest, friction must balance weight 10 N , but available friction is only 9 N , so the block slides down; the "block will remain stationary" statement is false (Reason false).

Assertion : Friction opposes motion of a body.
Reason : Static friction is self adjusting while kinetic friction is constant.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Check assertion
- Friction opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion at the contact, not "motion of a body" in every situation; for example, while walking, friction aids forward motion, so the blanket statement is false.
Check reason
- Static friction adjusts up to its limiting value to match the applied force, whereas kinetic friction is approximately constant during sliding, making the reason correct.

questions.solution:
Tension variation
- With unequal pulls at the ends (2 F at A and F at B) on a rope on a smooth table, the internal tension must vary linearly from 2F near A down to F near B to satisfy equilibrium of each small rope element.
On massless string claim
- Saying the situation becomes indeterminate for a massless string is a separate fact often discussed in assertion-reason keys for this problem; both I and II are marked true, but II is not the explanation for I in standard solutions.

questions.q:
Assertion : In the system of two blocks of equal masses as shown, the coefficient of friction between the blocks (\(\mu_2\)) is less than coefficient of friction (\(\mu_1\)) between lower block and ground.
For all values of force \(F\) applied on upper block lower block remains at rest.
Reason : Frictional force on lower block due to upper block is not sufficient to overcome the frictional force on lower block due to ground.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Why assertion is true
- For two equal-mass blocks, the maximum static friction at the ground is \(\mu 1(2 \mathrm{mg})\), which exceeds any friction demand transmitted from the top block because \(\mu 2 \lt  \mu 1\) limits the interface force first. Hence, the lower block can remain at rest for all applied F.
Why reason is correct

If both Assertion and Reason are false

- Even when the string is not accelerating as a whole, tension in a string with its own mass is generally non-uniform because different elements must support different portions of the string's weight or transmit different internal forces; only an ideal massless string has uniform tension.
Why reason is false
- Describing tension as an "electromagnetic force" is inaccurate in this context; tension is a contact force arising from internal stresses in the material and is not classified as a fundamental electromagnetic force in mechanics treatments.

questions.q: Two masses of $3\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$ are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is released from rest. What is the distance travelled by the heavier mass in the first $2\text{ seconds}$? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
The acceleration $a$ of an Atwood machine with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_1 \gt m_2$) is given by:
$a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$

Substituting the given values ($m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 2\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
$a = \dfrac{3 - 2}{3 + 2} \times 10 = \dfrac{1}{5} \times 10 = 2\text{ m/s}^2$

The system starts from rest, so initial velocity $u = 0$. The distance $s$ travelled in time $t = 2\text{ s}$ is:
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (2)^2$
$s = 4\text{ m}$

Answer: $4\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is placed on a frictionless inclined plane making an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. A constant external force of $21 \mathrm{~N}$ is applied on the block directed up the incline. If the block accelerates down the incline at $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, what is the value of $m$? (Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block be $m$.

The forces acting on the block along the inclined plane are:
1. The component of its weight acting down the incline: $m g \sin 30^{\circ}$
2. The external force acting up the incline: $F = 21 \mathrm{~N}$

Since the block accelerates down the incline at $a = 2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, the net force is directed downwards along the incline.

According to Newton's second law:
$m g \sin 30^{\circ} - F = m a$

Substituting the given values ($g = 10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, $\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5$):
$m(10)(0.5) - 21 = m(2)$
$5m - 21 = 2m$
$3m = 21$
$m = 7 \mathrm{~kg}$

Note: If the block were accelerating up the incline, the equation would be $F - m g \sin 30^{\circ} = m a$, which would yield $m = 3 \mathrm{~kg}$.

Answer: $7 \mathrm{~kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $5 \text{ kg}$ is placed on a rough inclined plane which makes an angle of $37^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. It is connected by a light string passing over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass $10 \text{ kg}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the $5 \text{ kg}$ block and the incline is $0.25$. Find the acceleration of the system when released from rest. (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = 0.8$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass on the incline be $m_1 = 5 \text{ kg}$ and the hanging mass be $m_2 = 10 \text{ kg}$.

The driving force pulling the system is the weight of the hanging mass:
$W_2 = m_2 g = 10 \times 10 = 100 \text{ N}$.

The forces opposing the motion of the $5 \text{ kg}$ block up the incline are the component of its weight parallel to the incline and the kinetic friction.
Component of weight down the incline: $m_1 g \sin 37^{\circ} = 5 \times 10 \times 0.6 = 30 \text{ N}$.

The normal force on the block is $N = m_1 g \cos 37^{\circ} = 5 \times 10 \times 0.8 = 40 \text{ N}$.
The kinetic friction force is $f_k = \mu_k N = 0.25 \times 40 = 10 \text{ N}$.

The net force accelerating the system is:
$F_{\text{net}} = W_2 - m_1 g \sin 37^{\circ} - f_k$
$F_{\text{net}} = 100 - 30 - 10 = 60 \text{ N}$.

The total mass of the system is $m_1 + m_2 = 5 + 10 = 15 \text{ kg}$.

The acceleration of the system is:
$a = \dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{60}{15} = 4.00 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Answer: $4.00 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The maximum horizontal acceleration a trolley can have without a block slipping on its floor is independent of the mass of the block.
Reason (R): The limiting static friction force between the block and the trolley floor is independent of the mass of the block.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
In the non-inertial frame of the accelerating trolley, a pseudo force $F_p = ma$ acts on the block of mass $m$ in the direction opposite to the acceleration $a$.

The limiting static friction force opposing this tendency to slip is $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$.

For the block not to slip, the pseudo force must be less than or equal to the limiting static friction:
$ma \le \mu_s mg$
$a \le \mu_s g$

The maximum acceleration is $a_{\text{max}} = \mu_s g$, which is independent of the mass $m$ of the block. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

The limiting static friction force is $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s mg$, which is directly proportional to the mass of the block. Therefore, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $m$ and $3m$ are placed in contact with each other on a smooth horizontal surface. In the first case, a horizontal force $F$ is applied to the block of mass $m$ to push the two-block system. In the second case, the same horizontal force $F$ is applied to the block of mass $3m$ from the opposite direction to push the system. The ratio of the normal contact force between the blocks in the first case to that in the second case is:
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the system in both cases be $a$.

Since the total mass is $4m$ and the applied force is $F$, the acceleration is $a = \dfrac{F}{4m}$.

In the first case, the force $F$ is applied to mass $m$. The block of mass $m$ pushes the block of mass $3m$. The only horizontal force on the $3m$ block is the contact force $N_1$.
Applying Newton's second law to the $3m$ block:
$N_1 = 3m \cdot a = 3m \left(\dfrac{F}{4m}\right) = \dfrac{3F}{4}$.

In the second case, the force $F$ is applied to mass $3m$. The block of mass $3m$ pushes the block of mass $m$. The only horizontal force on the $m$ block is the contact force $N_2$.
Applying Newton's second law to the $m$ block:
$N_2 = m \cdot a = m \left(\dfrac{F}{4m}\right) = \dfrac{F}{4}$.

The ratio of the contact forces is:
$\dfrac{N_1}{N_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3F}{4}}{\dfrac{F}{4}} = \dfrac{3}{1}$.

Therefore, the ratio is $3 : 1$.

Answer: $3 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity-time graphs of a block sliding from rest down a perfectly smooth incline and a rough incline (both having an angle of inclination of $30^{\circ}$ and the same length) are plotted. Both graphs are straight lines passing through the origin. If the ratio of the slope of the graph for the smooth incline to that of the rough incline is $2$, find the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough incline.
questions.solution:
The slope of a velocity-time graph represents the acceleration of the object.

Let $a_S$ be the acceleration on the smooth incline and $a_R$ be the acceleration on the rough incline. We are given:
$\dfrac{a_S}{a_R} = 2$

The acceleration of a block on a smooth incline of angle $\theta$ is:
$a_S = g\sin\theta$
For $\theta = 30^{\circ}$:
$a_S = g\sin 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{g}{2}$

The acceleration on a rough incline is:
$a_R = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$
For $\theta = 30^{\circ}$:
$a_R = g\left(\sin 30^{\circ} - \mu_k\cos 30^{\circ}\right) = g\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \mu_k\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

Substitute these into the ratio:
$\dfrac{\dfrac{g}{2}}{g\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \mu_k\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = 2$

Cancel $g$ and simplify the denominator:
$\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\dfrac{1}{2}(1 - \mu_k\sqrt{3})} = 2$
$\dfrac{1}{1 - \mu_k\sqrt{3}} = 2$

Rearranging the equation:
$1 = 2(1 - \mu_k\sqrt{3})$
$1 = 2 - 2\mu_k\sqrt{3}$
$2\mu_k\sqrt{3} = 1$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A uniform ladder rests against a smooth vertical wall and a rough horizontal floor. A person climbs up the ladder from the bottom to the top. Consider the following four statements regarding the forces acting on the ladder as the person ascends:

I. The normal reaction from the floor increases.
II. The normal reaction from the wall increases.
III. The friction force exerted by the floor increases.
IV. The ladder is most likely to slip when the person is near the bottom.

How many of the given statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the ladder be $m$ and the mass of the person be $M$.

Statement I is incorrect: For vertical equilibrium, the normal reaction from the floor is $N_{\text{floor}} = (m + M)g$, which remains constant regardless of the person's position.

Statement II is correct: Taking torque about the bottom of the ladder, $N_{\text{wall}} \times L \sin\theta = mg \dfrac{L}{2} \cos\theta + Mg x \cos\theta$, where $x$ is the distance of the person from the bottom. As $x$ increases, $N_{\text{wall}}$ must increase to maintain equilibrium.

Statement III is correct: For horizontal equilibrium, the friction force from the floor is $f = N_{\text{wall}}$. Since $N_{\text{wall}}$ increases, the required friction force also increases.

Statement IV is incorrect: Because the required friction force increases as the person climbs higher, the ladder is most likely to reach its limiting friction and slip when the person is near the top, not the bottom.

Thus, exactly two statements (II and III) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks $A$ and $B$ of masses $3\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$ respectively are placed in contact on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force of $25\text{ N}$ is applied on block $A$ towards the right, and a horizontal force of $5\text{ N}$ is applied on block $B$ towards the left. What is the magnitude of the normal contact force between the two blocks?
questions.solution:
Let the common acceleration of the system be $a$ towards the right.

The net external force on the system is $F_{\text{net}} = 25 - 5 = 20\text{ N}$.

Total mass of the system is $m_{\text{total}} = 3 + 2 = 5\text{ kg}$.

Acceleration $a = \dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4\text{ m/s}^2$.

Now, consider the free-body diagram of block $B$ ($2\text{ kg}$). The horizontal forces acting on it are the normal contact force $N$ towards the right and the applied force of $5\text{ N}$ towards the left.

Applying Newton's second law for block $B$:
$N - 5 = m_B \cdot a$
$N - 5 = 2 \times 4$
$N = 8 + 5 = 13\text{ N}$.

Answer: $13\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a 'death well' (a vertical cylindrical wall used for motorcycle stunts), a heavier motorcyclist requires a significantly greater minimum speed to prevent slipping downwards compared to a lighter motorcyclist.

Reason (R): The normal reaction force provided by the wall of the death well is directly proportional to the mass of the motorcyclist.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
For a motorcyclist in a death well, the normal reaction $N$ provides the necessary centripetal force: $N = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$. For a given speed $v$ and radius $R$, the normal force is directly proportional to the mass $m$. Hence, Reason (R) is true.

The frictional force $f$ acts upwards to balance the weight: $f = mg$.

For the motorcyclist not to slip downwards, $f \le \mu N \Rightarrow mg \le \mu \left(\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\right)$.

The mass $m$ cancels out from both sides, giving the condition for minimum speed as $v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{gR}{\mu}}$.

Since the minimum speed is independent of the mass, a heavier motorcyclist does not require a greater minimum speed. Hence, Assertion (A) is false.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train starts from rest and moves on a straight horizontal track with uniform acceleration. It covers a distance of $40$ m in $4$ s. A box resting on the floor of the train is observed to be just on the verge of slipping. What is the coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor of the train? (Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the train be $a$.

Using the second equation of motion:
$S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$40 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times a \times (4)^2$
$40 = 8a \Rightarrow a = 5$ m s$^{-2}$

For the box to be just on the verge of slipping, the pseudo force on it in the frame of the train must be equal to the limiting static friction.
$ma = \mu_s mg$
$\mu_s = \dfrac{a}{g}$

Substituting the values:
$\mu_s = \dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of mass $10$ kg is placed on the horizontal surface of a flatbed truck. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.4$. If the truck accelerates forward at $3$ m s$^{-2}$, what is the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the block?
(Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The limiting static friction force is given by:

$f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s mg$

$f_{s,\text{max}} = 0.5 \times 10 \times 10 = 50$ N

The force required to accelerate the block along with the truck is:

$F_{\text{req}} = ma = 10 \times 3 = 30$ N

Since the required force ($30$ N) is less than the limiting static friction ($50$ N), the block does not slip relative to the truck.

Static friction is self-adjusting and will exactly match the required force to keep the block at rest relative to the truck.

Therefore, the actual frictional force acting on the block is $30$ N.

Answer: $30$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A block takes twice the time to slide down a rough $45^{\circ}$ inclined plane as compared to a perfectly smooth $45^{\circ}$ inclined plane of the same length. The coefficient of kinetic friction for the rough plane is $0.75$.

Reason (R): The coefficient of kinetic friction between two given surfaces is independent of the macroscopic area of contact.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: Let the length of the incline be $L$. The acceleration on the smooth incline is $a_S = g \sin 45^{\circ}$. The acceleration on the rough incline is $a_R = g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$.

Using $L = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$, we get $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a}}$.

Given $t_R = 2 t_S$, we have:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a_R}} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a_S}}$
$\Rightarrow a_S = 4 a_R$

Substituting the accelerations:
$g \sin 45^{\circ} = 4 g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$

Since $\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ}$, this simplifies to:
$1 = 4(1 - \mu_k)$
$\Rightarrow 1 = 4 - 4\mu_k \Rightarrow 4\mu_k = 3 \Rightarrow \mu_k = 0.75$.

Reason (R) is true: The laws of friction state that the coefficient of kinetic friction is independent of the apparent macroscopic area of contact between the surfaces.

However, Reason (R) does not explain Assertion (A), as the calculation of $\mu_k$ depends on the kinematic relationship between time and acceleration ($t \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$), not on the area of contact.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a block on a rough horizontal surface pulled by a hanging mass via a string and pulley, if the horizontal surface is made completely smooth, the tension in the connecting string will decrease.
Reason (R): Removing friction increases the acceleration of the system, and for the hanging mass, the tension is given by $T = m_2(g - a)$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block on the surface be $m_1$ and the hanging mass be $m_2$.

The equation of motion for the hanging mass is:
$m_2 g - T = m_2 a$
Rearranging this gives the tension in the string:
$T = m_2(g - a)$

When the horizontal surface is rough, there is an opposing frictional force $f_k$, and the acceleration is $a = \dfrac{m_2 g - f_k}{m_1 + m_2}$.

When the surface is made completely smooth, the opposing friction $f_k$ becomes zero. The net driving force on the system increases, which causes the acceleration $a$ of the system to increase.

Looking at the relation $T = m_2(g - a)$, as the acceleration $a$ increases, the term $(g - a)$ decreases. Consequently, the tension $T$ in the string decreases.

Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason provides the correct physical explanation for the Assertion.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform plank of mass $10 \text{ kg}$ and length $4 \text{ m}$ rests horizontally on two supports placed exactly at its ends A and B. A block of mass $20 \text{ kg}$ is placed on the plank at a distance of $1 \text{ m}$ from end A. The magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by the support at end B is (take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let $N_A$ and $N_B$ be the normal reactions at supports A and B respectively.

The forces acting on the plank are:
1. Weight of the plank, $W_p = 10 \times 10 = 100 \text{ N}$, acting at its center of mass ($2 \text{ m}$ from end A).
2. Weight of the block, $W_b = 20 \times 10 = 200 \text{ N}$, acting at $1 \text{ m}$ from end A.
3. Upward normal reactions $N_A$ and $N_B$ at the ends.

For rotational equilibrium, the net torque about any point must be zero. Taking torque about end A to eliminate $N_A$:
$\Sigma \tau_A = 0$
$N_B \times 4 - W_p \times 2 - W_b \times 1 = 0$
$N_B \times 4 = (100 \times 2) + (200 \times 1)$
$N_B \times 4 = 200 + 200$
$4 N_B = 400$
$N_B = 100 \text{ N}$

The normal reaction at support B is $100 \text{ N}$. (Calculating the reaction at end A instead would give $200 \text{ N}$, and ignoring the mass of the plank would give $50 \text{ N}$).

Answer: $100 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In an Atwood machine consisting of two unequal masses connected by a light string over a smooth pulley, the tension in the string is greater than the weight of the heavier mass and less than the weight of the lighter mass.

Reason (R): The heavier mass accelerates downwards, meaning the net force on it is downwards, while the lighter mass accelerates upwards, meaning the net force on it is upwards.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Let the heavier mass be $m_1$ and the lighter mass be $m_2$.

For the heavier mass $m_1$, it accelerates downwards. The equation of motion is:
$m_1g - T = m_1a \Rightarrow T = m_1(g - a)$
This shows that the tension $T$ is strictly less than the weight of the heavier mass ($T \lt m_1g$).

For the lighter mass $m_2$, it accelerates upwards. The equation of motion is:
$T - m_2g = m_2a \Rightarrow T = m_2(g + a)$
This shows that the tension $T$ is strictly greater than the weight of the lighter mass ($T \gt m_2g$).

Therefore, Assertion (A) is incorrect.

Reason (R) correctly states the directions of acceleration and net force for both masses, which is the underlying physics principle used to derive the equations above. Thus, Reason (R) is correct.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hollow cylindrical drum of radius $0.5\text{ m}$ is placed inside an elevator that is accelerating upwards at $5\text{ m s}^{-2}$. A block is in contact with the inner vertical wall of the drum. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $0.2$. If the drum rotates about its vertical axis, what is the minimum angular velocity required to keep the block stationary relative to the drum? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
In the frame of the accelerating elevator, the block experiences a downward pseudo force $ma$ in addition to its weight $mg$.

Effective downward force $= m(g + a) = m(10 + 5) = 15m$.

The normal reaction $N$ from the wall provides the necessary centripetal force: $N = m\omega^2 R$.

To prevent the block from slipping downwards, the limiting static friction must balance the effective downward force: $f_{\text{max}} = \mu N = m(g+a)$.

Substituting $N$:
$\mu (m\omega^2 R) = m(g+a)$

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g+a}{\mu R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{15}{0.2 \times 0.5}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{15}{0.1}} = \sqrt{150} = 5\sqrt{6}\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Using only $g$ instead of $g+a$ leads to the incorrect answer $10\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, and subtracting the acceleration ($g-a$) leads to $5\sqrt{2}\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $5\sqrt{6}\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the physical situations involving a block of mass $m$ on a smooth inclined plane of angle $\theta$ (List-I) with their corresponding expressions (List-II).

List-IList-II
A. Acceleration of a block sliding freely down the inclineI. $mg \cos\theta$
B. Normal reaction on a block sliding freely down the inclineII. $g \sin\theta$
C. Minimum horizontal force required to keep the block stationaryIII. $\dfrac{mg}{\cos\theta}$
D. Normal reaction on a block kept stationary by a horizontal forceIV. $mg \tan\theta$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
A. For a block sliding freely down a smooth incline, the only force along the incline is $mg \sin\theta$. Acceleration $a = \dfrac{mg \sin\theta}{m} = g \sin\theta$.

B. The force perpendicular to the incline is balanced. Normal reaction $N = mg \cos\theta$.

C. To keep the block stationary with a horizontal force $F$, the component of $F$ up the incline must balance the weight component down the incline: $F \cos\theta = mg \sin\theta \Rightarrow F = mg \tan\theta$.

D. The normal reaction in this case balances both the perpendicular component of weight and the perpendicular component of the horizontal force: $N = mg \cos\theta + F \sin\theta$. Substituting $F = mg \tan\theta$, we get $N = mg \cos\theta + (mg \tan\theta) \sin\theta = mg \left(\cos\theta + \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) = \dfrac{mg}{\cos\theta}$.

Therefore, the correct match is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small coin is placed on a horizontal gramophone record that is rotating at a constant angular speed $\omega$. The coefficient of static friction between the coin and the record is $\mu_s$. If the acceleration due to gravity is $g$, what is the maximum distance from the centre at which the coin can be placed without slipping?
questions.solution:
For a coin on a horizontal rotating record, the normal force is $N = mg$.

The necessary centripetal force for the coin to move in a circle of radius $r$ is provided by static friction, so $f = m\omega^2 r$.

To prevent the coin from slipping, the required friction must not exceed the limiting static friction:
$f \le \mu_s N$
$m\omega^2 r \le \mu_s mg$

Solving for $r$, we get the maximum distance:
$r \le \dfrac{\mu_s g}{\omega^2}$

Thus, the maximum distance from the centre is $\dfrac{\mu_s g}{\omega^2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_s g}{\omega^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane with an initial velocity of $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The angle of inclination of the plane is $30^\circ$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. The distance travelled by the block along the incline before coming to a momentary rest is (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
When the block moves up the incline, both the component of gravity along the incline and the kinetic friction act downwards along the incline, opposing the motion.

The magnitude of retardation of the block is given by:
$a = g \sin \theta + \mu_k g \cos \theta$

Substituting the given values:
$a = 10 \sin 30^\circ + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} (10) \cos 30^\circ$
$a = 10 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
$a = 5 + 5 = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Using the third equation of motion, $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$:
$0 = (10)^2 - 2(10)s$
$20s = 100 \Rightarrow s = 5 \text{ m}$

Answer: $5 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A flatbed truck carrying a crate is moving at a steady speed of $15 \text{ m/s}$. The driver applies the brakes to stop the truck. If the coefficient of static friction between the crate and the truck bed is $0.3$, what is the minimum stopping distance of the truck such that the crate does not slide forward? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
When the truck decelerates, a pseudo force acts on the crate in the forward direction. To prevent the crate from sliding, the pseudo force must not exceed the maximum static friction.

Let the maximum deceleration of the truck be $a$.
$ma \le \mu_s mg$
$a \le \mu_s g$
$a_{\text{max}} = 0.3 \times 10 = 3 \text{ m/s}^2$

Using the third equation of motion to find the minimum stopping distance $S$:
$v^2 = u^2 - 2aS$
$0 = (15)^2 - 2(3)S$
$6S = 225$
$S = \dfrac{225}{6} = 37.5 \text{ m}$

The minimum stopping distance is $37.5 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $37.5 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a block of mass $m$ is placed on a rough inclined plane of angle $\theta$ such that $\tan \theta \lt \mu_s$ (where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction), the net force on the block is zero.
Reason (R): The limiting value of static friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction acting on the block.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For Assertion (A): The condition $\tan \theta \lt \mu_s$ implies that the angle of inclination $\theta$ is less than the angle of repose. In this condition, the component of weight along the incline ($mg \sin \theta$) is less than the limiting static friction ($\mu_s mg \cos \theta$). The block will not slide and remains in static equilibrium. Hence, the net force on the block is zero. Assertion (A) is correct.

For Reason (R): The limiting value of static friction is indeed directly proportional to the normal reaction ($f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N$). Reason (R) is a correct statement.

However, Reason (R) alone does not explain Assertion (A). The correct explanation for (A) is that static friction is a self-adjusting force that balances the applied force ($mg \sin \theta$) when the block is not on the verge of sliding. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three blocks of masses $2\text{ kg}$, $3\text{ kg}$, and $5\text{ kg}$ are connected in sequence by massless strings on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force of $40\text{ N}$ is applied to the $5\text{ kg}$ block, pulling the system forward. What is the tension in the string connecting the $2\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ blocks?
questions.solution:
The total mass of the system is $m_{\text{total}} = 2\text{ kg} + 3\text{ kg} + 5\text{ kg} = 10\text{ kg}$.

The common acceleration of the system is given by Newton's second law:
$a = \dfrac{F}{m_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$

To find the tension in the string connecting the $2\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ blocks, we isolate the trailing block ($2\text{ kg}$). The only horizontal force acting on it is the tension $T$.

Applying Newton's second law to the $2\text{ kg}$ block:
$T = m \times a = 2 \times 4 = 8\text{ N}$

Answer: $8\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is hinged at one end to a vertical wall. It is held in a horizontal position by a massless string attached to its other end. The string makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the rod. The magnitude of the net reaction force exerted by the hinge on the rod is:
questions.solution:
Taking torque about the hinge to be zero for rotational equilibrium:
$T \sin(30^{\circ}) \times L = Mg \times \dfrac{L}{2}$
$T \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{Mg}{2} \Rightarrow T = Mg$

For translational equilibrium, balancing the horizontal forces:
$H_x = T \cos(30^{\circ}) = Mg \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Balancing the vertical forces:
$H_y + T \sin(30^{\circ}) = Mg$
$H_y + Mg \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = Mg \Rightarrow H_y = \dfrac{Mg}{2}$

The net reaction force exerted by the hinge is the vector sum of its components:
$R = \sqrt{H_x^2 + H_y^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}Mg}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{Mg}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}M^2g^2 + \dfrac{1}{4}M^2g^2} = Mg$

Answer: $Mg$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block is held against the vertical front wall of a cart. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $0.4$. What is the minimum horizontal acceleration with which the cart must move forward so that the block does not slide down the wall?
(Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block be $m$ and the acceleration of the cart be $a$.

In the reference frame of the accelerating cart, a pseudo force $ma$ acts on the block, pressing it against the vertical wall. This provides the normal force:

$N = ma$

The maximum static friction force available to prevent the block from falling is:

$f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s ma$

For the block not to slide down, this upward frictional force must balance the downward gravitational force:

$\mu_s ma \ge mg$

$a \ge \dfrac{g}{\mu_s}$

Substituting the given values $\mu_s = 0.4$ and $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$:

$a_{\text{min}} = \dfrac{10}{0.4} = 25$ m s$^{-2}$

Answer: $25$ m s$^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is projected up a rough inclined plane of angle $45^{\circ}$ with an initial velocity. The time taken by the block to slide back down to its starting point is twice the time it took to slide up to the highest point. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the inclined plane is:
questions.solution:
Let the distance from the starting point to the highest point be $s$.

For the upward motion, the acceleration (deceleration) is:
$a_{\text{up}} = g(\sin 45^{\circ} + \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$

For the downward motion, the acceleration is:
$a_{\text{down}} = g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$

Using the kinematic equation $s = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$ (which is valid for upward motion if time is measured in reverse from the highest point), we have:
$s = \dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{up}} t_{\text{up}}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{down}} t_{\text{down}}^2$

Given that $t_{\text{down}} = 2 t_{\text{up}}$, we can substitute this into the equation:
$a_{\text{up}} t_{\text{up}}^2 = a_{\text{down}} (2 t_{\text{up}})^2$
$\Rightarrow a_{\text{up}} = 4 a_{\text{down}}$

Substituting the expressions for acceleration:
$g(\sin 45^{\circ} + \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ}) = 4 g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$

Since $\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, we can divide both sides by $g \cos 45^{\circ}$:
$1 + \mu_k = 4(1 - \mu_k)$
$\Rightarrow 1 + \mu_k = 4 - 4\mu_k$
$\Rightarrow 5\mu_k = 3 \Rightarrow \mu_k = 0.60$

A common mistake is forgetting to square the time ratio, which leads to $a_{\text{up}} = 2 a_{\text{down}}$ and an incorrect answer of $0.33$.

Answer: $0.60$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $3 \text{ kg}$ is pressed against a rough vertical wall by a horizontal force of $100 \text{ N}$. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $0.5$. If $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, what is the magnitude of the frictional force exerted by the wall on the block?
questions.solution:
The normal force $N$ exerted by the wall on the block is equal to the applied horizontal force.

$N = 100 \text{ N}$

The maximum possible static friction (limiting friction) is:

$f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = 0.5 \times 100 \text{ N} = 50 \text{ N}$

The downward force acting on the block due to gravity is:

$mg = 3 \text{ kg} \times 10 \text{ m s}^{-2} = 30 \text{ N}$

Since the required force to hold the block in equilibrium ($30 \text{ N}$) is less than the maximum static friction ($50 \text{ N}$), the block does not slip. Static friction is a self-adjusting force and will exactly balance the downward weight.

Therefore, the actual frictional force acting on the block is $30 \text{ N}$.

Answer: $30 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $8 \text{ kg}$ is placed on a rough horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley to a hanging block of mass $2 \text{ kg}$. When the system is released from rest, it accelerates at $1 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the $8 \text{ kg}$ block and the table? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block on the table be $m_1 = 8 \text{ kg}$ and the hanging mass be $m_2 = 2 \text{ kg}$.

The driving force for the system is the weight of the hanging mass: $W_2 = m_2 g = 2 \times 10 = 20 \text{ N}$.

The opposing force is the kinetic friction on the $8 \text{ kg}$ block: $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k (m_1 g) = \mu_k (8 \times 10) = 80 \mu_k$.

According to Newton's second law for the entire system:
Net force $= (m_1 + m_2) a$
$m_2 g - f_k = (m_1 + m_2) a$
$20 - 80 \mu_k = (8 + 2) \times 1$
$20 - 80 \mu_k = 10$
$80 \mu_k = 10$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{10}{80} = 0.125$

The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.125$.

Answer: $0.125$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $4\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$ are placed in contact with each other on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to the $4\text{ kg}$ block, pushing the system forward. If the contact force between the two blocks is $12\text{ N}$, what is the magnitude of the applied force $F$?
questions.solution:
Let the applied force be $F$ and the common acceleration of the system be $a$.

The force $F$ is applied to the $4\text{ kg}$ block, which in turn pushes the $2\text{ kg}$ block. The only horizontal force acting on the $2\text{ kg}$ block is the contact force $N$ from the $4\text{ kg}$ block.

Given $N = 12\text{ N}$, we can find the acceleration of the $2\text{ kg}$ block (and thus the whole system):
$a = \dfrac{N}{m_2} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Now, applying Newton's second law to the entire system to find the applied force $F$:
$F = (m_1 + m_2) \times a = (4 + 2) \times 6 = 6 \times 6 = 36\text{ N}$

Answer: $36\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is placed against the vertical front surface of a cart. The cart is accelerating horizontally forward. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and the vertical surface is $0.25$, what is the minimum acceleration of the cart required to prevent the block from falling down? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the cart be $a$.

In the reference frame of the cart, a pseudo force $ma$ acts on the block in the backward direction, pressing it against the vertical surface. Thus, the normal reaction is $N = ma$.

The frictional force acting upwards to prevent the block from falling is $f = \mu_s N = \mu_s ma$.

For the block to not fall, the frictional force must balance its weight:
$f \ge mg$
$\mu_s ma \ge mg$
$a \ge \dfrac{g}{\mu_s}$

Substitute the given values:
$a_{\text{min}} = \dfrac{10}{0.25} = 40 \text{ m/s}^2$.

Answer: $40 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ (where $m_1 \gt  m_2$) are connected by a light inextensible string that passes over a frictionless pulley. If the acceleration of the system is $\dfrac{g}{2}$, what is the ratio of their masses ($m_1 : m_2$)?
questions.solution:
For an Atwood machine with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_1 \gt m_2$), the acceleration $a$ is given by:

$a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$

Given that $a = \dfrac{g}{2}$, we can write:

$\dfrac{g}{2} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$

Cancelling $g$ from both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

Cross-multiplying yields:

$m_1 + m_2 = 2m_1 - 2m_2$

Rearranging the terms:

$3m_2 = m_1$

$\dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{3}{1}$

Thus, the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ is $3 : 1$.

Answer: $3 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $3 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed on a frictionless inclined plane of angle $30^{\circ}$. It is connected to a hanging block of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline. When the system is released from rest, what is the acceleration of the blocks? (Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the common acceleration of the system and $T$ be the tension in the string.

For the hanging block of mass $M = 2 \mathrm{~kg}$, the weight acts downwards ($M g = 20 \mathrm{~N}$).
For the block of mass $m = 3 \mathrm{~kg}$ on the incline, the component of weight acting down the incline is $m g \sin 30^{\circ} = 3(10)(0.5) = 15 \mathrm{~N}$.

Since $20 \mathrm{~N} \gt 15 \mathrm{~N}$, the $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ block will accelerate downwards and the $3 \mathrm{~kg}$ block will accelerate up the incline.

Writing the equations of motion for both blocks:
For the $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ block: $20 - T = 2a$
For the $3 \mathrm{~kg}$ block: $T - 15 = 3a$

Adding the two equations to eliminate $T$:
$(20 - T) + (T - 15) = 2a + 3a$
$5 = 5a$
$a = 1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$

Answer: $1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is sliding down a rough inclined plane of inclination $30^{\circ}$ with a constant acceleration of $2.5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. If $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is:
questions.solution:
The equation of motion for a block sliding down a rough inclined plane is given by:

$mg \sin \theta - f_k = ma$

where $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k mg \cos \theta$.

Substituting the expression for kinetic friction:

$mg \sin \theta - \mu_k mg \cos \theta = ma$

Dividing the entire equation by $m$:

$g \sin \theta - \mu_k g \cos \theta = a$

Substitute the given values ($g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, $a = 2.5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$):

$10 \sin 30^{\circ} - \mu_k (10) \cos 30^{\circ} = 2.5$

$10 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - \mu_k (10) \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 2.5$

$5 - 5\sqrt{3} \mu_k = 2.5$

$5\sqrt{3} \mu_k = 5 - 2.5 = 2.5$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{2.5}{5\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $4 \text{ kg}$ is pulled up along a rough inclined plane of angle $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal by a force of $70 \text{ N}$ acting parallel to the plane. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, what is the acceleration of the block? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Forces acting on the block along the inclined plane are:
1. Applied force $F = 70 \text{ N}$ (upwards)
2. Component of weight $mg \sin 30^{\circ}$ (downwards)
3. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k mg \cos 30^{\circ}$ (downwards)

Calculating the downward forces:
$mg \sin 30^{\circ} = 4 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 20 \text{ N}$
$f_k = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 4 \times 10 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 30 \text{ N}$

Net force acting up the plane:
$F_{\text{net}} = F - (mg \sin 30^{\circ} + f_k)$
$F_{\text{net}} = 70 - (20 + 30) = 20 \text{ N}$

Using Newton's second law:
$a = \dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Answer: $5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ is placed on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$. The acceleration of the system in terms of acceleration due to gravity ($g$) is:
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the system be $a$ and the tension in the string be $T$.

For the hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$, the equation of motion is:
$1g - T = 1a$

For the block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ on the smooth horizontal table, the driving force is only the tension:
$T = 4a$

Adding the two equations, we get:
$1g = (1 + 4)a$
$g = 5a$
$a = \dfrac{g}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{g}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block slides down a perfectly smooth inclined plane of angle $\theta$ in time $t$. If the same inclined plane is made rough with a coefficient of kinetic friction given by $\mu_k = \dfrac{8}{9}\tan\theta$, the time taken by the block to slide down the same distance from rest is $nt$. Find the value of $n$.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the inclined plane be $s$.

For the smooth inclined plane, the acceleration of the block is:
$a_S = g\sin\theta$
The time taken is $t$, so:
$s = \dfrac{1}{2}a_S t^2$

For the rough inclined plane, the acceleration is:
$a_R = g\sin\theta - \mu_k g\cos\theta$
Substituting $\mu_k = \dfrac{8}{9}\tan\theta$:
$a_R = g\sin\theta - \left(\dfrac{8}{9}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) g\cos\theta$
$a_R = g\sin\theta - \dfrac{8}{9}g\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}g\sin\theta$

The time taken on the rough incline is $nt$, so:
$s = \dfrac{1}{2}a_R (nt)^2$

Equating the two expressions for $s$:
$\dfrac{1}{2}a_S t^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}a_R (nt)^2$
$\Rightarrow n^2 = \dfrac{a_S}{a_R}$
$\Rightarrow n^2 = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{\dfrac{1}{9}g\sin\theta} = 9$
$\Rightarrow n = 3$

Thus, the value of $n$ is $3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $4\text{ kg}$ block rests on a rough horizontal surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction of $0.5$. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley to a hanging $6\text{ kg}$ block. If the system is released from rest, what is the distance descended by the hanging block in the first $2\text{ s}$? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the system be $a$ and the tension in the string be $T$.

For the hanging block ($6\text{ kg}$), the driving force is its weight:
$m_2 g = 6 \times 10 = 60\text{ N}$
The equation of motion is:
$60 - T = 6a$

For the block on the horizontal surface ($4\text{ kg}$), the opposing kinetic friction is:
$f_k = \mu_k m_1 g = 0.5 \times 4 \times 10 = 20\text{ N}$
The equation of motion is:
$T - 20 = 4a$

Adding the two equations to find the common acceleration:
$60 - 20 = (6 + 4)a$
$40 = 10a \Rightarrow a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Now, using the kinematic equation for uniformly accelerated motion to find the distance traveled in $t = 2\text{ s}$:
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
Since the system is released from rest, $u = 0$:
$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(4)(2)^2 = 8\text{ m}$

The hanging block descends by $8\text{ m}$.

Answer: $8\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A box placed on a flatbed truck will slide forward relative to the truck if the truck accelerates forward with an acceleration greater than $\mu_s g$.

Reason (R): The maximum static friction between the box and the truck floor cannot provide an acceleration greater than $\mu_s g$ to the box.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is false. When the truck accelerates forward, the pseudo force on the box acts in the backward direction relative to the truck. If the truck's acceleration exceeds the maximum acceleration that static friction can provide, the box will slide backward, not forward, relative to the truck.

Reason (R) is true. The only horizontal force acting on the box in the ground frame is static friction. The maximum static friction is $f_{s,max} = \mu_s mg$. Therefore, the maximum acceleration it can provide to the box is $a_{max} = \dfrac{\mu_s mg}{m} = \mu_s g$.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod is placed leaning against a smooth vertical wall and resting on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the rod and the floor is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$. What is the minimum angle the rod can make with the horizontal floor without slipping?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the rod be $m$, its length be $L$, and the angle it makes with the horizontal floor be $\theta$.

The forces acting on the rod are:
1. Weight $mg$ acting vertically downwards from the center of mass ($L/2$ from either end).
2. Normal reaction from the floor $N_f$ acting vertically upwards.
3. Normal reaction from the wall $N_w$ acting horizontally outwards.
4. Static friction $f$ acting horizontally inwards at the floor.

For translational equilibrium:
$\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow N_f = mg$
$\Sigma F_x = 0 \Rightarrow f = N_w$

For rotational equilibrium, taking torque about the point of contact with the floor:
$N_w \times L \sin\theta - mg \times \dfrac{L}{2} \cos\theta = 0$
$N_w = \dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta}$

Since $f = N_w$, the required friction force is $f = \dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta}$.

To prevent slipping, the friction force must not exceed the limiting static friction:
$f \le \mu N_f$
$\dfrac{mg}{2 \tan\theta} \le \mu mg$
$\dfrac{1}{2 \tan\theta} \le \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$
$\tan\theta \ge \sqrt{3}$

The minimum angle $\theta$ is therefore $60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $5 \text{ kg}$ is in contact with the inner wall of a hollow cylindrical drum of radius $2 \text{ m}$. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the inner wall is $0.5$. The cylinder is vertical and rotates about its axis at an angular velocity of $2\sqrt{10} \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. What is the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the block? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The normal force acting on the block provides the necessary centripetal force:
$N = m\omega^2 R$
$N = 5 \times (2\sqrt{10})^2 \times 2 = 5 \times 40 \times 2 = 400 \text{ N}$

The maximum possible static friction (limiting friction) is:
$f_{max} = \mu N = 0.5 \times 400 = 200 \text{ N}$

The downward gravitational force on the block is its weight:
$W = mg = 5 \times 10 = 50 \text{ N}$

Since the required upward force to keep the block stationary ($50 \text{ N}$) is less than the maximum available static friction ($200 \text{ N}$), the block will not slip.

Static friction is self-adjusting and will only act with the magnitude necessary to balance the applied forces. Therefore, the actual frictional force acting on the block is exactly equal to its weight, which is $50 \text{ N}$.

Answer: $50 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A flatbed truck carrying a heavy crate is travelling on a straight horizontal road at a speed of $20$ m/s. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the truck bed is $0.5$. What is the minimum stopping distance of the truck such that the crate does not slide forward on the truck bed during braking?
(Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the maximum deceleration of the truck without the crate sliding be $a$.

In the frame of the decelerating truck, a pseudo force $ma$ acts on the crate in the forward direction.

To prevent sliding, this pseudo force must be balanced by the static friction force acting in the backward direction.

The maximum static friction force available is $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$.

Equating the pseudo force to the maximum static friction force:
$ma = \mu_s mg$
$a = \mu_s g = 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ m/s$^2$

The truck must decelerate at a maximum of $5$ m/s$^2$ to prevent the crate from sliding.

Using the third equation of motion to find the minimum stopping distance $s$:
$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$
$0 = (20)^2 - 2(5)s$
$10s = 400$
$s = 40$ m

Answer: $40$ m

options: If both the assertion and reason are true and reason is a correct explanation of the assertion.
If both assertion and reason are true but assertion is not a correct explanation of the assertion.
If the assertion is true but the reason is false.
If both assertion and reason are false.
questions.solution: When brakes are on, there is no rolling of the wheels and the wheels slide. The sliding friction is greater than the rolling friction. Thus it is difficult to move a cycle along the road with its breaks on.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 0.5 kg for 0.25 s starting from rest. What is its momentum now?
questions.solution: Given, $\mathrm{F}=10 \mathrm{~N}, \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{i}}=0, \mathrm{~m}=0.5 \mathrm{~kg}, \Delta \mathrm{t}=0.25 \mathrm{~s}\because$ Change in momentum, $\Delta \mathrm{p}=\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}\begin{aligned} \because & \Delta \mathrm{p} & =\mathrm{F} \cdot \Delta \mathrm{t} \\ & & \mathrm{F} \cdot \Delta \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text { or } & & 10 \times 0.25 & =\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}-0.5 \times 0 \\ \text { or } & & \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}} & =2.5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A box of mass 8 kg is placed on a rough inclined plane of inclination $30^{\circ}$. Its downward motion can be prevented by applying a horizontal force F , then value of F for which friction between the block and the incline surface is minimum, is

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of 0.5 kg collided with wall at $30^{\circ}$ and bounced back elastically. The speed of ball was $12 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The contact remained for 1 s . What is the force applied by wall on ball?
questions.solution: Given, $\mathrm{m}=0.5 \mathrm{~kg}, \mathrm{v}=12 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, \Delta \mathrm{t}=1 \mathrm{~s}, \theta=30^{\circ}$ Force applied by wall on ball, $\mathrm{F}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{p}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$ or $\quad \mathrm{F}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}\right)_{\mathrm{H}}-\left(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)_{\mathrm{H}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$ In this elastic collision, final and initial velocity will be same but direction will changed. $\therefore$ Horizontal component, $\left(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{f}}\right)_{\mathrm{H}}=\mathrm{mv} \cos \theta$ and $\left(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)_{\mathrm{H}}=-\mathrm{mv} \cos \theta\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{mv} \cos \theta-(-\mathrm{mV} \cos \theta)}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{mV} \cos \theta}{\Delta \mathrm{t}} \\ & =\frac{2 \times 0.5 \times 12 \times \cos 30^{\circ}}{1}=6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~N} \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A skier starts from rest at point $A$ and slides down the hill without turning or breaking. The friction coefficient is $\mu$. When he stops at point $B$, his horizontal displacement is $S$. What is the height difference between points $A$ and $B ?$
(The velocity of the skier is small so that the additional pressure on the snow due to the curvature can be neglected. Neglect also the friction of air and the dependence of $\mu$ on the velocity of the skier.)
questions.solution: According to question, the situation is shown in the figure For a sufficiently safe-horizontal displacement $\Delta S$ can be considered straight. If the corresponding length of path element is $\Delta L$, the friction force is given by $\mu_{m g} \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta L}$ and the work done by the friction force equals force times displacement $\mu_{m g} \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta L} \Delta L=\mu_{m g} \Delta S$ Adding up, we find that along the whole path the total work done by the friction force is $\mu_{m g} s$. By energy conservation this must equals the decrease mgh in potential energy of skier. Hence, $h=\mu S$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The upper half of an inclined plane of inclination $\theta$ is perfectly smooth while the lower half rough. A block starting from rest at the top of the plane will again come to rest at the bottom if the coefficient of friction between the block and the lower half of the plane is given by
questions.solution: Suppose length of plane is $L$. When block descends the plane, rise in kinetic energy $=$ fall in potential energy $=m g L \sin \theta i$ Work done by friction $=\mu \times$ (reaction $) \times$ distance $\begin{aligned} 0+\mu(m g \cos \theta) & \times(L / 2) \\ & =\mu(m g \cos \theta) \times(L / 2)\end{aligned}$ Now, work done $=$ change in KE $\begin{array}{rlrl} & & m g L \sin \theta=\mu(m g \cos \theta) \times(L / 2) \\ \Rightarrow & \tan \theta=\mu / 2 \\ \therefore & \mu=2 \tan \theta\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long block $A$ of mass $M$ is at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. A small block $B$ of mass $M$ / 2 is placed on $A$ at one end and projected along $A$ with some velocity $v$. The coefficient of friction between the block is $\mu$. Then, the accelerations of blocks $A$ and $B$ before reaching a common velocity will be respectively
questions.solution:
The force causing the motion of $A$ is frictional force between $A$ and $B$,
So, acceleration of $A\mu M_B g=M_A a_A\Rightarrow a_A=\mu\left(\frac{M_B}{M_A}\right) g=\frac{\mu g}{2} \text { (towards right) }$
Block $B$ experiences frictions force toward left
$M_B a_B=\mu M_B g \Rightarrow a_B=\mu g \text { towards left }$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two masses 10 kg and 20 kg respectively are connected by a massless spring as shown in figure. A force of 200 N acts on the 20 kg mass. At the instant shown is figure the 10 kg mass has acceleration of $12 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. The value of acceleration of 20 kg mass is
questions.solution:
Equation of motion of $m_1=10 \mathrm{~kg}$ mass is $F_1=m_1 a_1=10 \times 12=120 \mathrm{~N}$
Force on 10 kg -mass is 120 N to the right. As action and reaction are equal and opposite, the reactions force $F$-on 20 kg mass $F=120 \mathrm{~N}$ to the left.
$\therefore$ Equation of motion of mass $m_2=20 \mathrm{~kg}$ is
$\begin{aligned} 200-F & =20 a_2 \\ 200-120 & =20 a_2 \\ 20 a_2 & =80 \\ a_2=\frac{80}{20} & =4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mass of a proton is 1847 times that of an electron. A electron and a proton are injected into a uniform electric field at right angle to the direction of the field with the same initial K.E.
options: the electron trajectory will be less curved than the proton trajectory.
both the trajectories will be straight.
the proton trajectory will be less curved than the electron trajectory.
both the trajectories will be equally curved.
questions.solution:
$K=\frac{1}{2} m V^2$. In electric field,
$Y=\frac{q E X^2}{2 m V^2}=\frac{q E X^2}{4 K}$
The curvature of the trajectory is proportional to $q E / K$. Since $q, E$ and $K$ are same for both particles, hence the trajectories will have the same curvature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body at rest slides down a $30^{\circ}$ inclined plane. The time taken by it to slide down is twice the time it takes when it slides down the same distance in the absence of friction. The coefficient of friction between the body and the inclined plane is
questions.solution: When a plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\theta$, which is greater than the angle of repose, then the body placed on the inclined plane slides down with an acceleration a. From figure, $R=m g \cos \theta$.....(i) Net force on the body down the inclined plane $f=m g \sin \theta-F$....(ii) i.e. $\quad f=m a=m g \sin \theta-\mu R \quad\left[\because \mu=\frac{F}{R}\right]\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad m a & =m g \sin \theta-\mu m g \cos \theta \quad \text { [from Eq. (i)] } \\ & =m g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta) \\ \Rightarrow \quad a & =g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta)\end{aligned}$ Time taken by the body to slide down the plane $\begin{aligned} & t_1=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{(g \sin \theta-\mu g \cos \theta)}} \\ & t_2=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta}} \quad \text { [in absence of friction] }\end{aligned}\because \quad t_1=2 t_2\Rightarrow \quad t_1^2=4 t_2^2$ [given] $\begin{aligned} & \left|\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{(g \sin \theta-\mu g \cos \theta)}}\right|^2=4 \times\left|\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta}}\right|^2 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 s}{g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta)}=4 \times \frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad \sin \theta=4 \sin \theta-4 \mu \cos \theta \\ \Rightarrow & \mu=\frac{3}{4} \tan \theta=\frac{3}{4} \tan 30^{\circ}=0.43\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light string passes over a frictionless pulley. To one of its ends a mass of 8 kg is attached. To its other end two masses of 7 kg each are attached. The acceleration of the system will be
questions.solution: From free body diagram of body $A$, $m_1 a=T_1-m_1 g$....(i) For body $B$, $m_2 \mathrm{a}=m_2 g+T_2-T_1$...(ii) For body C, $m_3 a=m_3 g-T_2$....(iii) On solving Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get $a=\frac{\left[\left(m_2+m_3\right)-m_1\right] g}{m_1+m_2+m_3}$ As, $\quad \begin{aligned} m_1 & =8 \mathrm{~kg}, m_2=m_3=7 \mathrm{~kg} \\ a & =\frac{6}{22} \mathrm{~g}=0.27 \mathrm{~g}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle slides down on a smooth incline of inclination $30^{\circ}$, fixed in an elevator going up with an acceleration $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. The box of incline has a length 4 m . The time taken by the particle to reach the bottom will be
questions.solution: In the frame of elevator, $a=$ acceleration of the particle with respect to the elevator $\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad m \sin 30(g+2) & =m a \\ a & =(g+2) \sin 30^{\circ} \\ & =(10+2) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & =6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\end{aligned}\therefore$ The distance travelled by the particle from the top to the bottom, $\begin{aligned} d & =\frac{4}{\cos 30^{\circ}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3} / 2}=\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3} \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { Using } s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2,\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & & \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3} & =0 \times t+\frac{1}{2} 6 t^2 \\ \Rightarrow & & t^2 & =\frac{16 \sqrt{3}}{3 \times 6} \\ \therefore & & t & =\frac{4}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \mathrm{~s}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is moving along a rough horizontal surface with an initial velocity of $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. If the body comes to rest after travelling a distance of 12 m , then the coefficient of sliding friction will be
questions.solution:
Given, $u=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}, s=12 \mathrm{~m}, v=0$
By third equation of motion,
$\begin{aligned} v^2 & =u^2-2 a s \\ 0 & =(10)^2-2 \times a \times 12 \\ 24 a & =100 \\ a & =4.17 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\end{aligned}$
Coefficient of sliding friction is given by
$\mu=\frac{a}{g}=\frac{4.17}{10}=0.41$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass 2 kg is pushed against a rough vertical wall with a force of 40 N , coefficient of static friction being 0.5. Another horizontal force of 15 N , is applied on the block in a direction parallel to the wall. If the block will move, then its direction would be
questions.solution:
The net force $=\sqrt{20^2+15^2}-0.5 \times 40\begin{aligned} & =25-20=5 \mathrm{~N} \\ & \therefore \quad \tan \theta=\frac{20}{15}=\frac{4}{3} \\ & \therefore \quad \theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)=53^{\circ} \\ & \end{aligned}$
So, the block will move at an angle $53^{\circ}$ with the 15 N force.

questions.q: A pendulum having a bob of mass $m$ is hanging in a ship sailing along the equator form east to west. When the strip is stationary with respect to water, the tension in the string is $T_0$. The difference between $T_0$ and earth attraction on the bob, is
questions.solution:
Speed of ship due to rotation of the earth $v=\omega R$
The net force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block slides down on an incline of angle $30^{\circ}$ with an acceleration $\frac{g}{4}$. Find the kinetic friction coefficient.
questions.solution: Consider the situation Let the mass of block be $m$. The equation of forces $\begin{aligned} m g \sin 30^{\circ}-f & =\frac{m g}{4} \\ f & =\frac{m g}{4}\end{aligned}$ Also, $N=m g \cos 30^{\circ}=m g \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ As the block is slipping on the incline, friction is $\begin{aligned} \mu_n & =\frac{F}{N}=\frac{m g}{4 m g \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monkey of mass 15 kg is climbing on a rope with one end fixed to the ceiling. If it wishes to go up with an acceleration $1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$, how much force should it apply to the rope if rope is 5 m long and the monkey starts from rest?
questions.solution:
The mass of monkey $=15 \mathrm{~kg}a=1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
For the motion of the monkey $T-[15 g-15(1)]=0$ Hence, $T$ is tension in the string $T=15 g+15\begin{aligned} T & =15(10+1)=15 \times 11 \\ & =165 \mathrm{~N}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block $B$ is pushed momentarily along a horizontal surface with an initial velocity $v$. If $\mu$ is the coefficient of sliding friction between $B$ and the surface, block $B$ will come to rest after a time
questions.solution:
Block will come to rest, if force applied on it. It will vanish due to frictional force acting between block $B$ and surface, i.e.,
Force applied $=$ Frictional force
i.e., $\quad \mu m g=m a$
or $\quad \mu m g=m\left(\frac{v}{t}\right)$ or $t=\frac{v}{\mu g}$

questions.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a circular track of radius 40 m. If the coefficient of friction is 1.28. The maximum velocity with which the car can be moved, is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { The maximum velocity } v_{\max }=\sqrt{\mu r g} \\ & =\sqrt{1.28 \times 40 \times 9.8} \\ & =22.4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three concurrent co-planar forces $1 \mathrm{~N}, 2 \mathrm{~N}$ and 3 N acting along different directions on a body
options: can keep the body in equilibrium if 2 N and 3 N act at right angle
can keep the body in equilibrium if 1 N and 2 N act at right angle
cannot keep the body in equilibrium
can keep the body in equilibrium in 1 N and 3 N act at an acute angle
questions.solution:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object start sliding on a frictionless inclined plane and from same height another object start falling freely.
options: both will reach with same speed
both will reach with same acceleration
both will reach in same time
questions.solution:
Here the potential energy will be converted to kinetic energy. Initially both the bodies have same potential energy. So finally both the bodies will have same kinetic energy.
⇒ So they will reach the ground with same speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The engine of a jet aircraft applies a thrown force of $10^5 \mathrm{~N}$ during take off and causes the plane to attain a velocity of $1 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$ in 10 s . The mass of the plane is
questions.solution:
Acceleration produced in jet
$=\frac{\text { Change in velocity }}{\text { Time }}a=\frac{\left(10^3-0\right)}{10}\therefore$ Mass $=\frac{\text { Force }}{\text { Acceleration }}=\frac{10^5}{10^2}=10^3 \mathrm{~kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone weighing 1 kg and sliding on ice with a velocity of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ is stopped by friction in 10 s . The force of friction (assuming it to be constant) will be
questions.solution: $u=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, \quad v=0, \quad f=0 \mathrm{~s}a=\frac{v-u}{t}=\frac{0-2}{10}=-\frac{2}{10}=-\frac{1}{5}=-0.2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\therefore$ Friction force $=m a=1 \times(-0.2)=-0.2 \mathrm{~N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet of mass 20 g and moving with $600 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ collides with a block of mass 4 kg hanging with the string. What is velocity of bullet when it comes out of block, if block rises to height 0.2 m after collision?
questions.solution:
According to conservation of linear momentum,
$m_1 v_1=m_1 v+m_2 v_2$
where $v_1$ is velocity of bullet before collision, $v$ is velocity of bullet after the collision and $v_2$ is the velocity of block.
$\therefore \quad 0.02 \times 600=0.02 v+4 v_2$
Here, $\quad v_2=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gh}}=\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 0.2}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\therefore \quad 0.02 \times 600=0.02 v+4 \times 2\Rightarrow \quad 0.02 v=12-8\Rightarrow \quad v=\frac{4}{0.02}=200 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A weightless thread can bear tension upto 37 N . A stone of mass 500 g is tied to it and revolved in a circular path of radius 4 m in a vertical plane. If $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$, then the maximum angular velocity of the stone will be
questions.solution:
Maximum tension in the thread is given by or
$T_{\max }=m g+\frac{m v^2}{r}$
or $\quad T_{\max }=m g+m r \omega^2(\because v=r \omega)$
or $\quad \omega^2=\frac{T_{\max }-m g}{m r}$
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& T_{\max }=37 \mathrm{~N}, m=500 \mathrm{~g}=0.5 \mathrm{~kg}, g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}, \\
& r=4 \mathrm{~m} \\
& \therefore \quad \omega^2=\frac{37-0.5 \times 10}{0.5 \times 4}=\frac{37-5}{2} \\
& \text { or } \quad \omega^2=16 \text { or } \omega=4 \mathrm{rad} \mathrm{s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

t & =\frac{v}{\mu g}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Diwali rocket is ejecting 50 g of gases $/ \mathrm{s}$ at a velocity of $400 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The accelerating force on the rocket will be
questions.solution:
The accelerating force on the rocket
$=\text { upward thrust }=\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t} \cdot u$
Given, $\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}=50 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{s}, v=400 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
So, accelerating force $=50 \times 10^{-3} \times 400=20 \mathrm{~N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which is true for rolling friction $\left(\mu_r\right)$, static friction $\left(\mu_s\right)$ and kinetic friction $\left(\mu_k\right)$ :
questions.solution:
Static friction is always greater than kinetic friction, and rolling friction is less than kinetic friction, so
$\mu_s \gt \mu_k \gt \mu_r$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A motor cycle is going on an overbridge of radius $R$. The driver maintains a constant speed. As the motor cycle is ascending on the overbridge, the normal force on it
questions.solution: Reaction of normal force on the motor cyclist $M g \cos \theta-N=\frac{m v^2}{R}$ or $\quad N=M g \cos \theta-\frac{M v^2}{R}$ As the motor cyclist moves upward on the bridge, $\theta$ decreases and therefore, $N$ increases and becomes maximum at the highest point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two weights $w_1$ and $w_2$ are suspended to the two strings on a frictionless pulley. When the pulley is pulled up with an acceleration $g$, then the tension in the string is :
questions.solution: Equation of motion for first weight $\begin{aligned} T-m_1 g & =m_1(g+a) \\ \Rightarrow \quad T-2 m_1 g & =m_1 a\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$ For second weight $\begin{aligned} m_2 g-T & =m_2(a-g) \\ 2 m_2 g-T & =m_2 a\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$ On solving Eqs. (1) and (2) $\begin{aligned} T & =\frac{4 m_1 m_2 g}{\left(m_1+m_2\right)} \\ & =\frac{4 w_1 w_2}{\left(w_1+w_2\right)}\end{aligned}$
